title: Linux Command Line Essentials
subtitle: Work confidently in a Linux terminal: move around the file system, manage files, permissions, software and processes, analyse text with pipes, write shell scripts and work on remote machines over SSH.
outcomes: Navigate the Linux file system and create, copy, move, find and delete files with confidence
Set file permissions and ownership, use sudo safely and install software with apt
Monitor and control processes and background jobs
Combine grep, sort, uniq, cut, wc, sed and awk with pipes to answer questions about logs and data
Write Bash scripts with arguments, checks, loops and exit statuses
Connect to and work on remote machines with SSH keys, and copy files securely
prerequisites: No Linux experience needed. You need a Linux system where you can install software: Ubuntu on WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) on Windows, an Ubuntu virtual machine (for example in VirtualBox), or a cloud server. The labs assume Ubuntu or Debian, which use apt; other distributions work with small changes.
description: Servers, containers, cloud machines and the computers that train AI models nearly all run Linux, and the people who build and run them work in its terminal. This course teaches the command line from the first prompt, on your own Linux system. You'll find your way around the file system and organise files; control who can read, change and run them; install software and keep an eye on running processes; and combine small tools such as grep, sort, uniq, cut, wc, sed and awk with pipes to answer real questions about a web server's log, including spotting someone probing for a login page. Then you'll put commands into Bash scripts that check their input and report errors properly, and run them on a remote machine over SSH, with key pairs instead of passwords. Every lesson shows the commands step by step, and every module ends with a lab on sample files that come with the course, with the exact output a correct answer prints.

modules.title: Find your way around the shell
modules.summary: Meet the terminal and the shell, move around the Linux file system, and create, copy, move, find and delete files and directories.

lessons.title: The shell, the terminal and commands
objectives: Explain what the terminal and the shell are
Run commands with options and arguments, and find help on any command
key_points: A terminal is the window you type in; the shell is the program that reads your commands and runs them. Bash is the default shell on most Linux distributions, including Ubuntu.
A command is a program's name followed by options, which change what it does, and arguments, which say what it works on: in ls -l /etc, ls is the command, -l an option and /etc an argument.
man ls opens the manual page for ls (q quits, / searches), and most commands print a short summary of their options with --help.
Tab completes command and file names, the Up arrow brings back earlier commands, history lists them, and Ctrl+R searches them as you type.
Linux is case-sensitive: Report.txt and report.txt are different files.
WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) runs a real Linux distribution, such as Ubuntu, alongside Windows; a virtual machine or a cloud server works just as well for this course.

steps.do: Open a terminal: on Ubuntu desktop press Ctrl+Alt+T; with WSL, open Ubuntu from the Start menu; on a cloud server, connect with your provider's instructions. Ask who and where you are.
steps.see: Your user name, the machine's name and /bin/bash.

steps.do: See which distribution and version you're running.
steps.see: Lines such as PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04 LTS".

steps.do: Get help on ls two ways: the short summary, then the full manual page. Press q to leave the manual.
Type ls /e and press Tab: the shell completes it to /etc/. Press Enter to list /etc.
steps.see: A long list of configuration files and directories.

steps.do: Run a command with an option and an argument, then look back through your history and search it with Ctrl+R (type 'os-' to find the head command).

lessons.title: Navigating the file system
objectives: Describe the Linux directory tree and the home directory
Move around with absolute and relative paths
key_points: Linux has a single tree of directories starting at the root, /. System settings live in /etc, programs in /usr/bin, logs in /var/log, and each user's files in their home directory, such as /home/amara, which ~ stands for.
pwd prints the working directory, the one you're in; cd changes it. cd on its own goes home, and cd - goes back to the previous directory.
An absolute path starts at /, as in /home/amara/project; a relative path starts from the working directory, as in project/data. . means the current directory and .. the one above it.
ls lists a directory: -l shows details such as permissions, owner, size and date, -a includes hidden files, whose names start with a dot, and -h shows sizes in K, M and G.
Put names with spaces in quotes, as in cd "My Files", or escape each space with a backslash; it's simpler not to use spaces in file names at all.

steps.do: Find out where you are, and list your home directory with its hidden files.
steps.see: /home/yourname, and entries such as . and .. and hidden files such as .bashrc.

steps.do: Jump to the system's log directory with an absolute path, and list it with readable sizes.
Go up one level with a relative path, then back to where you were.
steps.see: /var, then /var/log again.

steps.do: Go home, make a working folder for this course, and move into it.
steps.code:
cd
mkdir linux-lab
cd linux-lab
pwd
steps.see: /home/yourname/linux-lab

lessons.title: Working with files and directories
objectives: Create, copy, move, rename and delete files and directories
Use wildcards and find to work with many files at once
key_points: mkdir makes a directory, and mkdir -p also makes any missing parent directories; touch creates an empty file, or updates the time on an existing one.
cp copies (cp -r copies a directory and everything in it), and mv moves or renames: mv draft.txt final.txt renames a file where it is.
rm deletes files and rm -r deletes directories, with no recycle bin and no undo; rm -i asks before each deletion, and rmdir removes only empty directories.
cat prints a file, less pages through a long one (q quits), and head and tail show the first or last lines: tail -n 20 shows the last 20, and tail -f follows a file as it grows.
Wildcards match file names: * matches any characters and ? exactly one, so mv inbox/*.csv data/ moves every CSV file. The shell expands them before the command runs.
find searches a directory tree: find project -name '*.csv' lists the CSV files in it, and find project -type f lists every file. Its order isn't sorted, so pipe it to sort when order matters.

steps.do: In ~/linux-lab, make a small tree in one command, and some empty files.
steps.code:
mkdir -p practice/drafts practice/final
touch practice/drafts/a.txt practice/drafts/b.txt practice/drafts/notes.md

steps.do: Copy one file, move the text files with a wildcard, and rename one.
steps.code:

mv practice/drafts/*.txt practice/final/
mv practice/final/a.txt practice/final/report.txt

steps.do: List every file, sorted.
steps.see: practice/drafts/notes.md, practice/final/b.txt, practice/final/report.txt and practice/notes-copy.md

steps.do: Delete safely: rm -i asks before each file. Answer y, then remove the whole practice tree.
Read files: print a short one, page through a long one with less (q quits), and show the end of another.

modules.title: Permissions, software and processes
modules.summary: Control who can read, change and run files, use administrator rights safely to install software with apt, and watch, pause and stop running processes.

lessons.title: Owners and permissions
objectives: Read the permissions in ls -l
Set permissions with chmod, in numeric and symbolic form
key_points: Every file has an owner, a group and three sets of permissions, for the owner (u), the group (g) and everyone else (o): r to read, w to write and x to execute. ls -l shows them as, for example, -rwxr-x---.
On a directory, r lets you list what's in it, w lets you create and delete files in it, and x lets you enter it with cd and reach the files inside.
chmod changes permissions. In numeric form, each digit adds read (4), write (2) and execute (1) for the owner, the group and others: chmod 750 gives rwxr-x--- and chmod 600 gives rw-------.
In symbolic form, chmod u+x adds execute for the owner, chmod g+w adds write for the group, and chmod o-r takes read away from others.
Give the least access that works: 600 for private keys and secrets, 700 for private directories, and never 777, which lets anyone change the file.
chown changes a file's owner and group, as in sudo chown amara:staff report.txt, and needs administrator rights; stat -c '%A %a %n' file shows its permissions in both forms.

steps.do: Make a file and a directory in ~/linux-lab, and look at their permissions.
steps.code:
cd ~/linux-lab
touch plan.txt
mkdir vault
ls -ld plan.txt vault
steps.see: Something like -rw-rw-r-- for the file and drwxrwxr-x for the directory: the defaults depend on your system's umask.

steps.do: Set the file to 640 and check it in both forms.
steps.see: -rw-r----- 640 plan.txt

steps.do: Use symbolic form to take everything away from others on the directory, and check.
steps.see: The last three characters are now ---.

steps.do: See what x means on a directory: remove it for yourself, try to enter, then put it back. (Use your normal account: root ignores these permission checks.)
steps.code:
chmod u-x vault
cd vault
chmod u+x vault
steps.see: bash: cd: vault: Permission denied

steps.do: Look at the owner and group columns of a system file that only root can change.
steps.see: Owned by root, with no read permission for others: password hashes live there.

lessons.title: Administrator rights and installing software
objectives: Use sudo safely
Install, inspect and remove software with apt
key_points: root is the administrator account, allowed to do anything. sudo runs a single command as root, after asking for your own password, if your account is allowed to use it, and it logs what was run.

Use sudo only for commands that need it, such as installing software or changing system settings, and read a command carefully before you run it with sudo, because nothing stops root from damaging the system.
On Ubuntu and Debian, apt manages software: sudo apt update refreshes the list of available packages, sudo apt install tree installs one, and sudo apt upgrade installs updates for what's installed.
apt search finds packages, apt show describes one, sudo apt remove uninstalls one, and dpkg -s tree says whether a package is installed.

Packages come from repositories your system trusts, and apt checks their signatures; software downloaded from random websites skips those protections. Other distributions have their own package managers, such as dnf on Fedora.

steps.do: Refresh the package lists. sudo asks for your password; nothing appears as you type it.
steps.see: Lines such as Hit: and Get: for each repository, ending with how many packages can be upgraded.

steps.do: Look before you install.
steps.see: The package's version, size, dependencies and a short description.

steps.do: Install it, and check it's there.
steps.code:
sudo apt install -y tree
dpkg -s tree | grep Status
which tree
steps.see: Status: install ok installed, and /usr/bin/tree

steps.do: Try it on your lab folder.
See which installed packages have updates waiting, without installing them yet.

lessons.title: Processes and jobs
objectives: Find and inspect running processes
Run, pause, resume and stop jobs, and send signals
key_points: A process is a running program, with a process ID (PID). ps shows your terminal's processes, ps aux shows every process, and top shows them live, busiest first (q quits); htop is a friendlier version you can install.
Ctrl+C asks the program in the foreground to stop. Ctrl+Z pauses it; bg resumes it in the background, fg brings it back to the foreground, and jobs lists your background jobs.
Ending a command with & starts it in the background, as in sleep 300 &, so the terminal is free for other work.

kill sends a signal to a process, by PID or by job number (kill %1). The default signal, TERM, asks the program to finish cleanly; kill -9 sends KILL, which stops it at once with no chance to tidy up, so use it last.
pgrep -a sleep lists the PIDs and command lines of processes whose names match, which helps you find the one to stop.

steps.do: Start a long command in the foreground, then press Ctrl+Z to pause it.
steps.see: [1]+  Stopped                 sleep 600

steps.do: Resume it in the background, start another background job, and list them.
steps.see: [1]- Running sleep 600 & and [2]+ Running sleep 300 &

steps.do: Find their PIDs.
steps.see: Two lines, each a PID followed by the command, such as 4321 sleep 600.

steps.do: Bring job 1 back to the foreground, then stop it with Ctrl+C.
Stop job 2 with a TERM signal, then check.
steps.see: [2]+  Terminated              sleep 300

steps.do: Watch every process live with top, sorted by CPU use; press q to quit.

files.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Copy every .txt file in this folder into backups/, and say how many were copied.
mkdir -p backups
count=0
for file in *.txt; do
    cp "$file" backups/
    count=$((count + 1))
done
echo "Backed up $count file(s) to backups/"
The Wi-Fi password is not stored here.

hints: Each digit of a numeric mode is read (4) + write (2) + execute (1): 7 is rwx, 5 is r-x, 6 is rw- and 0 is ---.
If sudo says you're not in the sudoers file, your account can't use administrator rights: on your own machine, the account made when you installed Linux (or WSL) can.

modules.title: Pipes and text tools
modules.summary: Redirect input and output, chain small tools with pipes, and search, sort, count and reshape text with grep, sort, uniq, cut, wc, sed and awk.

lessons.title: Redirection and pipes
objectives: Send a command's output and errors to files
Chain commands together with pipes
key_points: Every command has three streams: standard input (0), standard output (1) and standard error (2), where error messages go. In a terminal, all three are the terminal itself.
> sends output to a file, replacing what was there; >> appends to it; < takes input from a file; 2> sends errors to a file; and 2>&1 sends errors to wherever the output is going.
A pipe, |, connects one command's output to the next command's input, so small tools combine into answers: cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c.
tee copies its input to a file and passes it on down the pipe, so you can save an intermediate result and keep going.
Careful with >: sort data.txt > data.txt empties the file before sort reads it. Write to a new file, then rename it.
/dev/null throws away anything written to it, so command 2> /dev/null hides error messages.

steps.do: Save a listing to a file, add to it, and count its lines.
steps.code:
cd ~/linux-lab
ls /etc > listing.txt
ls /usr/bin >> listing.txt
wc -l < listing.txt

steps.do: Separate output from errors: ls a directory that exists and one that doesn't.
steps.code:
ls /etc/hostname /nowhere > out.txt 2> errors.txt
cat out.txt
cat errors.txt
steps.see: /etc/hostname in out.txt, and ls: cannot access '/nowhere': No such file or directory in errors.txt

steps.do: Chain commands: how many entries in /etc are directories?
Save a step with tee and keep piping.
steps.see: A count on screen, and the full list saved in programs.txt.

lessons.title: Searching, sorting and counting
objectives: Find lines with grep
Rank and count values with sort, uniq, cut, wc and head
key_points: grep prints the lines that match a pattern: -i ignores case, -v prints the lines that don't match, -c counts matching lines, -n shows line numbers, and -E allows extended patterns such as ' (404|500) '.
sort sorts lines as text by default: -n sorts numerically, -r reverses the order, and -t, -k2 sorts on the second comma-separated field.
uniq only removes duplicate lines that are next to each other, so sort first. uniq -c puts a count before each line, and sort | uniq -c | sort -rn ranks values from most to least frequent.
cut picks out fields: cut -d' ' -f1 takes the first space-separated field, and cut -d, -f2,3 takes the second and third columns of a CSV file.
wc counts lines (-l), words (-w) and bytes (-c); reading from < file, as in wc -l < access.log, it prints just the number.
head -n 3 and tail -n 3 keep the first or last lines, which turns a ranked list into a top three.

steps.do: Download access.log from this module's lab into ~/linux-lab/logs and look at its first line. Each line is one request: IP address, time, request, status code and size.
Which requests failed with 404 Not Found?
steps.see: Five lines, for /wp-login.php and /old-page.html.

steps.do: How many requests were POSTs?
Who made the most requests? Build the pipeline one command at a time, running it after each addition.
steps.code: cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3

steps.do: Which pages were asked for, how often? Field 7 is the path.

lessons.title: Editing streams with sed and awk
objectives: Find and replace text with sed
Filter, pick out and add up fields with awk
key_points: sed edits text as it streams past: sed 's/old/new/' replaces the first match on each line, and sed 's/old/new/g' replaces every match.
sed -n '5,10p' prints only lines 5 to 10. sed -i edits a file in place, and GNU sed's -i.bak keeps a backup copy; run the command without -i first to check what it does.

awk splits each line into fields, $1, $2 and so on, on spaces by default or on another separator given with -F, and runs { action } on every line that matches an optional pattern, as in awk '$9 >= 400'.
awk keeps its variables from line to line, so awk '{sum += $10} END {print sum}' adds up a column; NR is the line number, and NR > 1 skips a header row.
Regular expressions describe patterns: ^ anchors the start of a line, $ the end, . matches any character and [0-9] a digit, and in extended syntax (grep -E, sed -E) + means one or more.
awk's for (key in array) loop visits keys in no particular order, so pipe its output through sort when order matters.

walkthrough.title: Reshape and total with sed and awk

sed -E 's/^[0-9.]+/x.x.x.x/' access.log > anon.log

Use awk to print the status code and path of every failed request.
steps.see: Eight lines: 404s for /wp-login.php and /old-page.html, a 403 for /admin and two 500s for /api/orders.

steps.do: Add up the bytes sent, in field 10.
Total the orders by region in a CSV file (download orders.csv from the lab), skipping the header and sorting the result.
steps.code: awk -F, 'NR > 1 {total[$2] += $3} END {for (r in total) printf "%s %.2f\n", r, total[r]}' orders.csv | sort

lab.title: Analyse a web server log
lab.goal: Answer questions about a made-up web server's access log, and a small CSV file of orders, with pipelines of grep, sort, uniq, cut, wc, sed and awk, including spotting a visitor probing for a login page.
setup: Download the starter files access.log and orders.csv into ~/linux-lab/logs

steps.do: Count the requests and the different visitors (IP addresses, field 1).
steps.code:
cd ~/linux-lab/logs
wc -l access.log
echo "Visitors: $(cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort -u | wc -l)"
steps.see: 40 access.log and Visitors: 6

steps.do: Rank the three busiest visitors.
steps.code: cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3

steps.do: Count each status code (field 9), most frequent first.
Which missing pages were asked for? Then find who asked for /wp-login.php: this site doesn't run WordPress, so those requests look like someone probing for a login page.
steps.code:
grep ' 404 ' access.log | cut -d' ' -f7 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
grep 'wp-login' access.log | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c
steps.see: 3 /wp-login.php and 2 /old-page.html, then the IP address that made the wp-login requests.

steps.do: Add up the bytes sent, and count the requests in each hour (the hour is the second field when you split on colons).
steps.code:
awk '{sum += $10} END {print sum}' access.log
cut -d: -f2 access.log | sort | uniq -c

steps.do: Make an anonymised copy for sharing, and check it.
steps.see: Both lines start with x.x.x.x - -

steps.do: Total the orders by region, then summarise all of them, with awk.
steps.code:
awk -F, 'NR > 1 {total[$2] += $3} END {for (r in total) printf "%s %.2f\n", r, total[r]}' orders.csv | sort
awk -F, 'NR > 1 {sum += $3; n++} END {printf "%d orders, total %.2f, average %.2f\n", n, sum, sum / n}' orders.csv
steps.see: east 63.75, north 95.74, south 103.00, west 60.60, then 10 orders, total 323.09, average 32.31

steps.do: Save your favourite pipeline's output to a file with tee as you run it, and write two sentences for the site's owner: what does the log show about the wp-login.php requests, and what would you do about them?

checks.text: The requests and visitors are counted.
The busiest visitors are ranked correctly.
The status codes are counted.
The missing pages are found.
The bytes and the requests per hour are right.
The log is anonymised with sed.
The orders are totalled by region and summarised with awk.
The note identifies 203.0.113.5 as the source of the wp-login.php requests and suggests a sensible defensive step, such as watching for it, rate limiting or blocking the address.

lab.submit: Paste each command and its output, and your two sentences for the site's owner.
hints: Build a pipeline one step at a time: run cut on its own, then add | sort, then | uniq -c, checking the output each time.
uniq -c only counts neighbouring duplicates, so always sort before it.
In awk, $9 is the ninth field: count them in the first line of the log to see why the status code is field 9 and the size field 10.

modules.title: Shell scripts and SSH
modules.summary: Turn commands into Bash scripts that take arguments, make decisions, loop and report errors properly, then run them on remote machines over SSH with key pairs.

lessons.title: Your first shell scripts
objectives: Write and run a Bash script with variables and arguments
Use exit statuses and safe settings to catch errors
key_points: A shell script is a text file of commands. Its first line, the shebang #!/usr/bin/env bash, says which program runs it, and chmod +x script.sh lets you run it as ./script.sh.
Variables are set with no spaces around =, as in name="Amara", and used as "$name". Quote them: an unquoted value with spaces is split into separate words.
$1, $2 and so on are the script's arguments, $# is how many there are and "$@" is all of them; $(command) puts a command's output into a variable or a string.
Every command ends with an exit status, kept in $?: 0 means success and anything else failure. exit 2 ends a script with status 2, and >&2 sends a message to standard error.
set -euo pipefail makes a script stop at the first failing command (-e), treat unset variables as errors (-u) and count a pipeline as failed if any part of it fails (-o pipefail).
shellcheck, which you can install with apt, reads a script and points out common mistakes, such as missing quotes.

walkthrough.title: Write, run and break a script

steps.do: Create greet.sh with a text editor such as nano (Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits).
Type the script.
steps.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

name="${1:-world}"
files=$(ls | wc -l)
echo "Hello, $name. This folder has $files entries."

steps.do: Make it executable and run it with and without an argument.
steps.see: Hello, world. ..., then Hello, Amara Okafor. ...

steps.do: Check the exit status of a command that works and of one that fails.
steps.see: 0, then 2

steps.do: Install shellcheck and let it review the script.

lessons.title: Decisions, loops and functions
objectives: Make decisions with if and tests
Repeat work with for and while loops, and organise it with functions
key_points: if [ -f "$file" ]; then ... fi runs commands only when a test succeeds: -f tests for a file, -d for a directory, -z for an empty string, and -eq, -ne, -lt and -gt compare numbers.
The spaces inside [ ] matter, because [ is itself a command; Bash's [[ ]] is a safer variant that copes with empty variables and supports pattern matching.
for log in logs/*.log; do ... done runs once for each matching file, and while read -r line; do ... done < file runs once for each line of a file.
A function groups commands under a name, as in count_errors() { awk '$9 >= 400' "$1" | wc -l; }; it takes its own arguments as $1, $2 and so on, and returns an exit status.
&& runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded, and || only if it failed: mkdir -p backups && cp *.txt backups/.

walkthrough.title: Loop over logs with a function

steps.do: In ~/linux-lab/logs, write a script, count.sh, with a function and a loop.
steps.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

count_errors() {
    awk '$9 >= 400' "$1" | wc -l
}

for log in *.log; do
    if [ -s "$log" ]; then
        echo "$log: $(count_errors "$log") errors"
    else
        echo "$log is empty"
    fi
done

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: One line per .log file, such as access.log: 8 errors.

steps.do: Make an empty log and run it again: -s tests for a file that exists and isn't empty.
steps.see: empty.log is empty

n=0
while read -r line; do
    n=$((n + 1))
    echo "$n: $line"
done < orders.csv

lessons.title: Remote machines with SSH
objectives: Connect to a remote machine with SSH and verify its identity
Log in with a key pair, configure shortcuts and copy files securely
key_points: SSH (Secure Shell) gives you an encrypted terminal on another machine: ssh amara@203.0.113.10 logs in as amara, and ssh host 'df -h' runs one command there and returns.

The first time you connect, SSH shows the server's key fingerprint and asks whether to trust it. Check it against the fingerprint the server's administrator gives you: SSH then remembers it in ~/.ssh/known_hosts and warns you if it ever changes.

Key pairs are safer than passwords: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 makes a private key, which never leaves your machine, and a public key (.pub), which ssh-copy-id adds to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Protect the private key with a passphrase.
SSH refuses to use a private key that other users can read: keep ~/.ssh at 700 and private keys at 600.
A Host entry in ~/.ssh/config saves typing: with its HostName, User and IdentityFile set, ssh lab is all you need to connect.

scp copies files over SSH, as in scp report.txt lab:/tmp/, and rsync -av copies only what's changed. On a server, once key logins work, setting PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config stops password-guessing attacks.

files.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Summarise a web server access log: requests, visitors, the busiest visitor and errors.
set -euo pipefail

# TODO: if the script wasn't given exactly one argument ($# is the number of arguments),
# print "Usage: $0 LOGFILE" to standard error (>&2) and exit with status 1

log="$1"

# TODO: if "$log" isn't a file ([ ! -f "$log" ]), print "No such file: $log" to standard error
# and exit with status 2

# TODO: fill in each variable with $( ... ), using the pipelines from module 3:
requests=   # the number of lines:  wc -l < "$log"
visitors=   # the number of different IP addresses (field 1)
busiest=    # the most frequent IP address and its count, like:  203.0.113.5 (12 requests)
            # hint: ... | sort -rn | awk 'NR == 1 {print $2 " (" $1 " requests)"}'
errors=     # the number of requests with a status code (field 9) of 400 or more

echo "Report for $log"
echo "Requests: $requests"
echo "Visitors: $visitors"
echo "Busiest visitor: $busiest"
echo "Errors (4xx and 5xx): $errors"

hints: Test the script's checks with [ "$#" -ne 1 ] and [ ! -f "$log" ]; with set -u, use "${1:-}" if you read $1 before checking $#.
If ssh asks for a password even after ssh-copy-id, check that ~/.ssh is 700 and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is 600 on the server.
If localhost refuses the connection, the SSH server isn't running: start it with sudo systemctl start ssh, or sudo service ssh start on WSL.

project.title: Automate a server log report
project.brief: You look after a small web server and want a daily summary of its logs without typing the same pipelines every morning. Write a Bash script, daily-report.sh, that takes a directory of access logs and writes one report per log into a reports directory: the number of requests and visitors, the three busiest visitors and most requested pages, the count of each status code, and a 'suspicious requests' section listing the IP addresses that asked for pages such as /wp-login.php or /admin and got 403 or 404 responses. The script must check its arguments, cope with a missing directory, an empty directory and an empty log with clear messages and sensible exit statuses, use functions, quote its variables and pass shellcheck. Then run it on a remote machine over SSH with key login and copy the reports back with scp or rsync. As a stretch, add a crontab line that would run it every morning.
deliverables: daily-report.sh, with comments and a usage message
The reports it writes for the sample logs (access.log and sunday.log from the module 4 lab)
A terminal session showing the script's error handling: no argument, a missing directory and an empty directory
A terminal session showing the script run over SSH and the reports copied back
README.md: how to install and run it, and what each section of the report means

rubric.name: Correct reports
rubric.description: Every count in the reports is right for the sample logs, including the busiest visitors, pages, status codes and the suspicious requests from 203.0.113.5.

rubric.name: Robust error handling
rubric.description: Missing or wrong arguments, a missing or empty directory and empty logs give clear messages on standard error and distinct non-zero exit statuses, never a crash halfway through.

rubric.name: Script quality
rubric.description: set -euo pipefail, functions that each do one job, quoted variables, readable names and comments; shellcheck reports nothing.

rubric.name: Working over SSH
rubric.description: The script runs on a remote machine with key-based login, the server's fingerprint was checked, and the reports are copied back with scp or rsync.

rubric.name: Documentation
rubric.description: The README explains installation, usage, the exit statuses and each report section clearly enough for a colleague to use the script.

project.submit: Paste daily-report.sh, one generated report, the shellcheck output, the terminal sessions for error handling and SSH, and your README.md.
